questions.prompt: Which level of protein structure refers to the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain?

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the supported answer. The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds, tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional fold of one chain, and quaternary structure requires more than one polypeptide subunit.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: D

questions.workedSolution: The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds, tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional fold of one chain, and quaternary structure requires more than one polypeptide subunit. Therefore the correct answer is A: Primary structure.

questions.prompt: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Which statement describes what happens?

options.label: A
options.text: Water leaves by osmosis and the cell becomes flaccid
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: B
options.text: Water enters by active transport and the cell bursts
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: C
options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid but does not burst
options.rationale: This is the supported answer. Pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the cell sap, so water moves into the cell by osmosis across the partially permeable membrane. The inelastic cellulose cell wall resists expansion and builds up pressure potential, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no net movement of water in either direction
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

questions.workedSolution: Pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the cell sap, so water moves into the cell by osmosis across the partially permeable membrane. The inelastic cellulose cell wall resists expansion and builds up pressure potential, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting. Therefore the correct answer is C: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid but does not burst.

questions.prompt: The sodium–potassium pump moves three Na⁺ ions out of a neurone and two K⁺ ions in for each ATP hydrolysed. What is the direct consequence of this stoichiometry?

options.label: A
options.text: The membrane potential across the membrane is abolished
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: B
options.text: The inside of the cell becomes more negative relative to the outside (the pump is electrogenic)
options.rationale: This is the supported answer. Each cycle of the pump moves a net one positive charge out of the cell (three Na⁺ out versus two K⁺ in), so the pump directly makes the inside more negative and contributes to the resting potential. The stoichiometry is fixed at 3:2, and the pump does not allow sodium to diffuse back through it.

options.label: C
options.text: Equal numbers of positive charges move in each direction
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: D
options.text: Sodium ions diffuse back into the cell through the pump
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

questions.workedSolution: Each cycle of the pump moves a net one positive charge out of the cell (three Na⁺ out versus two K⁺ in), so the pump directly makes the inside more negative and contributes to the resting potential. The stoichiometry is fixed at 3:2, and the pump does not allow sodium to diffuse back through it. Therefore the correct answer is B: The inside of the cell becomes more negative relative to the outside (the pump is electrogenic).

questions.prompt: A student investigates how substances cross cell surface membranes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term osmosis.
parts.correctAnswer: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to a region of lower (more negative) water potential across a partially permeable membrane, down the water potential gradient.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why active transport requires a supply of ATP.

parts.text: Describe the role of cholesterol in the cell surface membrane when the temperature falls.
parts.correctAnswer: Cholesterol sits between the phospholipid molecules and, at low temperatures, prevents the phospholipid tails packing too closely together, maintaining fluidity; it therefore buffers the membrane against temperature change and helps stabilise it.

questions.prompt: A metabolic poison allows protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing through ATP synthase, but does not block the electron transport chain. Predict the effect on respiration.

options.label: A
options.text: Oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis both stop immediately
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxygen consumption stops but ATP synthesis increases
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen consumption continues but much less ATP is synthesised
options.rationale: This is the supported answer. The leak uncouples oxidative phosphorylation: electrons still flow along the transport chain to oxygen, the final electron acceptor, so oxygen consumption continues. However, the proton gradient is dissipated without driving ATP synthase, so ATP yield falls sharply while glycolysis still regenerates NAD.

options.label: D
options.text: Glycolysis stops because NAD cannot be regenerated
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

questions.workedSolution: The leak uncouples oxidative phosphorylation: electrons still flow along the transport chain to oxygen, the final electron acceptor, so oxygen consumption continues. However, the proton gradient is dissipated without driving ATP synthase, so ATP yield falls sharply while glycolysis still regenerates NAD. Therefore the correct answer is C: Oxygen consumption continues but much less ATP is synthesised.

questions.workedSolution: Because the genetic code is (almost) universal, a bacterial ribosome translates human mRNA codons into exactly the same amino acid sequence as a human cell would, so the protein produced by the engineered bacteria is genuine human insulin. Therefore the correct answer is C: The genetic code is universal — the same codons specify the same amino acids in bacteria and humans.

questions.prompt: A student outlines how bacteria are genetically engineered to produce human insulin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the role of reverse transcriptase in obtaining the human insulin gene.
parts.correctAnswer: Reverse transcriptase synthesises a complementary DNA (cDNA) copy of the insulin gene from the mature mRNA extracted from pancreatic beta cells; this cDNA contains the coding sequence without introns, which bacteria cannot remove.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of DNA ligase in forming a recombinant plasmid.
parts.correctAnswer: DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of the insulin gene and the cut plasmid by catalysing the formation of phosphodiester bonds between their complementary sticky ends, sealing the gene into the plasmid to make recombinant DNA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of producing insulin from genetically modified bacteria rather than extracting it from animal pancreases.
parts.correctAnswer: Any one developed point, for example: the product is exact human insulin, so it is less likely to trigger an immune response than pig or cow insulin; or GM bacteria grow rapidly in fermenters, giving large, reliable and cheaper supplies without the use of animals.

questions.prompt: Which lymphocyte directly destroys body cells infected with a virus?

questions.prompt: Why must new influenza vaccines be developed on a regular basis?

options.label: A
options.text: Influenza viruses stop expressing antigens after each season
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: B
options.text: Vaccines lose all of their activity within a few months in the body
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: C
options.text: Memory cells permanently destroy the viral antigens
options.rationale: This option is a plausible misconception, but it conflicts with the principle established in the worked solution.

options.label: D
options.text: Antigenic variability — mutation changes the virus's surface antigens, so existing memory cells and antibodies no longer match
options.rationale: This is the supported answer. Influenza has an RNA genome that mutates readily (antigenic drift, and occasionally antigenic shift), altering its haemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface antigens. Memory cells from an earlier vaccination then fail to recognise the new variants, so vaccines are reformulated each season to match circulating strains.

Memory cells from an earlier vaccination then fail to recognise the new variants, so vaccines are reformulated each season to match circulating strains. Therefore the correct answer is D: Antigenic variability — mutation changes the virus's surface antigens, so existing memory cells and antibodies no longer match.

questions.prompt: A student compares the different ways in which the body is protected against infectious disease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between active and passive immunity.
parts.correctAnswer: In active immunity the person's own lymphocytes respond to an antigen and produce antibodies and memory cells, giving long-lasting protection; in passive immunity ready-made antibodies are received, for example across the placenta or in an antiserum, giving immediate but short-lived protection without memory cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of memory cells in the secondary immune response.
parts.correctAnswer: Memory B- and T-lymphocytes persist after a first infection; on re-exposure to the same antigen they clone rapidly and differentiate into plasma cells and effector T cells, so the antibody concentration rises faster and to a higher level than in the primary response.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viral diseases.
parts.correctAnswer: Antibiotics target structures or processes unique to bacteria, such as peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis or 70S ribosomes; viruses lack these targets and replicate inside host cells using the host’s machinery, so antibiotics cannot act on them.
